title: The Gassed Captain Who Hated the Straight Line
author: B. H. Liddell Hart
wiifm: When you are stuck, the obvious move is usually to push harder at the same wall. Basil Liddell Hart survived the Somme and spent his life arguing that this is almost always the wrong answer. Go round, he said: find the line of least expectation, unsettle your opponent before you strike, and aim for a better peace rather than a total victory. His ideas are powerful and widely used. But we will also follow a darker thread, because he polished his own legend in ways historians later exposed, and that is a lesson too.

ch.h: A minister's son at the Somme
b: Basil Henry Hart was born in Paris on 31 October 1895, the son of a Methodist minister serving the English-speaking congregation there. He added his mother's maiden name, Liddell, later, in 1921. He was a sickly, bookish boy who loved games and played war with toy soldiers, and he went up to Corpus Christi College, Cambridge, to read history in 1913.

His father hoped he might become a lawyer or a clergyman. At Cambridge he was, by his own later account, a middling student more interested in reading about past campaigns than in passing exams, and he never took his degree. The war arrived before he had to choose a career, and it chose one for him.

In August 1914 the First World War began. He was commissioned into the King's Own Yorkshire Light Infantry and went to France. He was hit by shellfire near Ypres in 1915, and returned to the front for the great offensive on the Somme in the summer of 1916.

On the first day of the Somme, 1 July 1916, the British army suffered about fifty seven thousand casualties, the worst day in its history, attacking straight into barbed wire and machine guns. Liddell Hart's battalion was badly mauled in those weeks. In mid July, around Mametz Wood, he was caught in a gas attack and invalided home. He would never fight again.

He did not at first turn against the generals. His early writing was rather admiring of Haig. The bitterness came later, as he studied the war and as the full scale of the losses sank in. But the image that stayed with him was the one every survivor carried: men walking forwards in straight lines into fire.
ch.cap: Men walk in straight lines into Somme wire and smoke

ch.h: From training manuals to the newspapers
b: After the war he was put to work writing infantry training manuals, and he developed an idea he called the expanding torrent. Instead of attacking evenly along a whole front, troops should probe for weak points, and when they found one, pour reserves through it, spreading out behind the enemy's line like water bursting through a dam.

Poor health ended his army career and he retired as a captain in 1927. But he had already found a better platform. From 1925 he was military correspondent of the Daily Telegraph, and from 1935 of The Times. He wrote fast, clearly and endlessly, and he became one of the most influential voices on defence in Britain.

Alongside the tank enthusiast J. F. C. Fuller, he argued that mechanised forces, tanks moving with motorised infantry and supported by aircraft, could restore movement to war and avoid another stalemate in the trenches. He wrote a biography of the Roman general Scipio Africanus, admiring how Scipio beat Hannibal not by facing him in Italy but by striking at Spain and then Carthage itself. That pattern of going round would become his life's theme.
ch.cap: Liddell Hart types his columns beside the torrent sketch

ch.h: Thirty wars and two hundred and eighty campaigns
b: In 1929 he published The Decisive Wars of History. He revised and expanded it several times, most importantly as Strategy: The Indirect Approach in 1954, and again as Strategy in 1967. The method was ambitious. He surveyed military history from the Greeks to the twentieth century, some thirty wars and, he said, about two hundred and eighty campaigns.

His conclusion was striking. In only a handful of them, he claimed six, had a decisive result followed a direct approach to the enemy's main army. In the great majority, victory came after some indirect approach that first threw the enemy off balance. The direct attack, he argued, tends to harden resistance, just as pushing on a door makes the person behind it push back.

Some of his examples are thrilling. Hannibal crossing the Alps into Italy in 218 BC, coming from the direction the Romans least expected, then luring a Roman army into an ambush along the shore of Lake Trasimene. The Byzantine general Belisarius in the sixth century, winning with small forces by tempting enemies to attack him on ground of his choosing. Scipio, refusing to fight Hannibal in Italy and instead taking the war to Spain and Africa, so that Carthage had to recall its great general to defend home.

Critics have pointed out that his classification is rather elastic. Almost any successful campaign can be described as indirect in hindsight, and his own definitions shift. So the statistics are better read as illustrations than proof. But the examples themselves are vivid, and they carry the argument.
ch.cap: Liddell Hart tallies 280 campaigns among open histories

b: So what is the indirect approach? At its core, it is a psychological idea. The aim of strategy, Liddell Hart wrote, is not so much to seek battle as to create a situation so advantageous that, if it does not produce the decision by itself, a battle will surely achieve it. In other words, do the real work before the fight.

He called this dislocation. Physically, you move against the enemy's rear, his supply lines or his line of retreat, so that his position no longer makes sense. Psychologically, you create the feeling in the enemy commander's mind that he is trapped. The two go together. A general who suddenly finds you behind him is beaten in his head before he is beaten on the field.

To achieve this, he said, you should follow the line of least expectation and the line of least resistance. They are usually the same thing. Where the enemy does not expect you, he is weakest. And he advised choosing a line of operation that offers alternative objectives, so the enemy cannot tell which one you are really after and must spread his defence.

His favourite examples included Sherman's march through Georgia in 1864, which bypassed Confederate armies to wreck the South's heartland, and General Allenby's campaign at Megiddo in 1918, which broke through on the coast and sent cavalry deep behind the Ottoman lines.

He boiled his advice down to eight maxims, six positive and two negative. Adjust your end to your means. Keep your object always in mind. Choose the line of least expectation. Exploit the line of least resistance. Take a line of operation that offers alternative objectives. Make sure your plans and dispositions are flexible and can adapt to circumstances. Then the two warnings. Do not throw your weight into a stroke while your opponent is on guard, ready to parry it. And do not renew an attack along the same line, or in the same form, after it has once failed. That last one is the Somme in a single sentence.
ch.cap: The arrow skirts the fortress to strike behind it

b: One friendship fed the theory more than any other. In the late 1920s Liddell Hart got to know T. E. Lawrence, Lawrence of Arabia, who had helped lead the Arab Revolt against the Ottoman Empire from 1916 to 1918. The two men corresponded at length, and in 1934 Liddell Hart published a book about him, later known as T. E. Lawrence in Arabia and After.

Lawrence's campaign seemed to prove the indirect approach on a small scale. Rather than throwing Arab irregulars against Turkish garrisons, Lawrence and his allies raided the Hejaz railway, blowing up track and trains, so the Turks had to spread thousands of men along hundreds of miles of desert to protect it. The garrison at Medina was left stranded, and the Arab forces moved north towards Damascus, appearing where they were least expected.

Lawrence himself had written that his aim was to make the enemy's army defend everything while his own forces attacked nothing in particular, striking and vanishing. Liddell Hart loved this. It was strategy as a contest of minds and of space, not of mass against mass.

Lawrence died after a motorcycle accident in Dorset in May 1935. Liddell Hart's admiring portrait helped to cement the Lawrence legend, and later historians have questioned parts of it, as they have questioned parts of Liddell Hart's own. But the idea he drew from the desert, that a weaker force can win by making a stronger one spread itself thin, has inspired insurgents and small companies alike.
ch.cap: Arab raiders on camels watch the Hejaz railway burn

ch.h: Grand strategy and the better peace
b: Liddell Hart insisted that strategy, in the military sense, sat inside something larger. He called it grand strategy: the use of all a nation's resources, economic, diplomatic, moral and military, to achieve the aims of policy. And he argued that the real object of war is a better state of peace, even if only from your own point of view.

This led him to attack total victory as a goal. If you destroy the enemy so completely that you exhaust yourself and poison the peace, you have lost even if you have won. The First World War had shown it. Britain won, but at a cost that left it weaker and set up the next war.

Here he aimed his heaviest fire at Clausewitz, whom he called the Mahdi of mass, blaming his followers for the doctrine of seeking the enemy's main army and destroying it whatever the cost. Most scholars now think this was a caricature. Clausewitz himself had insisted that politics must govern war. But Liddell Hart's attack did help to make limited aims and indirect methods respectable.

Later editions added a warning about guerrilla war. Liddell Hart had watched the Second World War encourage resistance movements across occupied Europe, and he worried that the habits of sabotage and lawlessness they encouraged did not simply vanish afterwards. Fighting by irregular methods, he argued, could leave a legacy of instability that poisoned the very peace the war was meant to secure.
ch.cap: Statesmen sign a peace meant to outlast the war

b: In 1937 and 1938 he became an unofficial adviser to the Secretary of State for War, Leslie Hore-Belisha, and pushed reforms in the British army, including mechanisation and promotion for younger officers. But he also advocated what he called limited liability, the idea that Britain should not send a large army to the continent again, and should rely on naval power, air power and allies.

His time as an adviser was brief and stormy. Senior officers resented a journalist with access to the minister, and by 1938 the arrangement had ended in bad feeling. Hore-Belisha himself was dismissed in January 1940. Liddell Hart went back to writing, now often from outside the tent, and increasingly critical of how the war was being run.

When war came in 1939, events went against him. In 1940 German armoured forces broke through the Ardennes, the line of least expectation, and raced to the Channel. In one sense this vindicated the ideas of mobile warfare he had championed. But Britain was unprepared for a major land war, partly because of the very policy he had urged.

During the war he also argued for a negotiated peace and against the bombing of German cities, positions that made him unpopular. Some of his criticism of area bombing has since been widely shared. But for a time he was out of favour with the establishment he had once advised.

There is a real irony here. The man who had preached avoiding a costly commitment to a continental army watched Britain forced into exactly that, first in 1940 and then on a vast scale from 1944. His defenders say his warnings about mass slaughter were right in spirit. His critics say that his advice had left the army smaller and less ready than it should have been. Both can be true. Ideas that are wise as a general habit can still be dangerous as a specific policy, if they are applied without asking what the opponent is actually doing.
ch.cap: German tanks burst from the Ardennes, the unexpected line

b: After the war Liddell Hart interviewed captured German generals and published the results in 1948 as The Other Side of the Hill. Many of them, including Heinz Guderian, the father of the German armoured force, said kind things about him. And here the story takes a turn.

When Guderian's memoir Panzer Leader came out in English in 1952, it contained a passage crediting Liddell Hart with having inspired German tank doctrine. That passage was not in the original German edition. In 1988 the American political scientist John Mearsheimer published Liddell Hart and the Weight of History, showing from Liddell Hart's own papers that he had encouraged Guderian to add it, even suggesting the wording.

Mearsheimer and others, including the historian Brian Bond, also argued that Liddell Hart had rewritten his own record. He had played down his early admiration for the British high command, overstated how clearly he had foreseen the blitzkrieg, and quietly revised his books after the event to look more prophetic. Some scholars think Mearsheimer was too harsh, but the core of the charge about Panzer Leader is generally accepted.

Mearsheimer also suggested a motive. By 1945 Liddell Hart's reputation was damaged by the policy of limited liability, and by his wartime calls for negotiation. Linking himself to the German armoured victories was a way of rebuilding it as the prophet of the blitzkrieg. Whatever the motive, it worked for decades.
It matters because his influence partly rested on this reputation. The man who taught that you should shape the other side's perceptions before a fight had, it turns out, been shaping ours.
ch.cap: A letter suggests the paragraph praising Liddell Hart

b: None of this means the ideas are worthless. The indirect approach has been read and used by commanders around the world. Israeli officers in the 1950s and 1960s, including Yigal Allon, admired his work. Business strategists borrowed his thinking about avoiding a competitor's strength and aiming at the gap.

The central insight is simple and durable. A direct assault on an opponent's strongest point usually produces the most resistance at the highest cost. Unsettle first: threaten more than one objective, move where you are not expected, make the other side's position stop making sense. Then strike. And keep in mind that the purpose of any contest is the peace that follows.

Liddell Hart was knighted in 1966 and died on 29 January 1970, at his home in Buckinghamshire. His books are still in print. The fairest verdict may be that he was a brilliant populariser and a sharp critic of the costly frontal attack, whose ideas were sometimes better than his honesty about where they came from.
ch.cap: The old captain reads in his Buckinghamshire garden

take: Direct attacks on a rival's strongest point harden resistance. Look for the market, channel or customer group where competitors are not expecting you.
Liddell Hart called it dislocation. Change the situation so your opponent's position stops making sense before you make the decisive move.
Follow the line of least expectation
Where the other side is not looking, it is usually weakest. Surprise is often cheaper than force.
A plan that threatens several objectives forces rivals to spread themselves. Keep options alive so you can switch to whichever proves weakest.
Winning a dispute so completely that you poison the relationship can be a loss. Decide what good looks like after the fight before you start it.
Grand strategy means using money, partnerships, reputation and persuasion, not just head-on competition.
Liddell Hart edited his own record and helped insert praise of himself into Guderian's memoir. Check claims about who foresaw what, including your own.
His count of indirect victories used elastic definitions. When evidence seems to prove your favourite idea perfectly, check how it was sorted.
recall: Avoiding a direct attack on the enemy's main strength and instead throwing him off balance physically and psychologically, by moving against his rear or along the line of least expectation. The decisive blow follows once he is dislocated.
What did Liddell Hart mean by grand strategy?
The coordination of all a nation's resources, economic, diplomatic, moral and military, towards the aims of policy. He argued its true object is a better state of peace.
His post-First World War idea that attackers should probe for weak points and then pour reserves through any gap, spreading behind the enemy line.
What did John Mearsheimer reveal in 1988?
That Liddell Hart had encouraged Guderian to add a passage praising him to the English edition of Panzer Leader, and had revised his own record to appear more prophetic.
Why did he call Clausewitz the Mahdi of mass?
He blamed Clausewitz's influence for the obsession with destroying the enemy's main army at any cost, as in the First World War. Most scholars think this misread Clausewitz.

words: To find a way round an obstacle rather than going through it.

A biography that treats its subject with uncritical reverence.

Acting to make yourself seem more important or impressive than you are.

Done or reasoned after the event, often in a way that fits the facts to a theory with hindsight.

stories: The paragraph that was not in the German edition

After the Second World War, Liddell Hart interviewed captured German generals, including Heinz Guderian, father of the panzer force. When Guderian's memoir Panzer Leader appeared in English in 1952, it contained a passage crediting Liddell Hart with inspiring German tank doctrine. The passage was not in the original German edition. In 1988 the political scientist John Mearsheimer showed from Liddell Hart's own papers that he had encouraged Guderian to add it, even suggesting the wording. Some historians think Mearsheimer was too harsh overall, but that core finding is generally accepted. The great preacher of shaping your opponent's perceptions had been shaping ours, and it worked for decades.
Blow up the railway, not the garrison

During the Arab Revolt of 1916 to 1918, T. E. Lawrence and his Arab allies faced Ottoman garrisons they could never beat head on. So they mostly left them alone and attacked the Hejaz railway instead, blowing up track and trains, forcing the Turks to spread thousands of men along hundreds of miles of desert. The garrison at Medina was left stranded while the Arab forces moved north towards Damascus. Lawrence wrote that the aim was to make the enemy defend everything while his own forces attacked nothing in particular. Liddell Hart, who befriended him, made this the small scale proof of his indirect approach.

Hannibal had been loose in Italy for years, beating Roman armies, after crossing the Alps from the direction Rome least expected. The young Roman general Scipio refused to chase him. Instead he took the war to Spain, then to Africa, threatening Carthage itself. Carthage had to recall Hannibal to defend home, and Scipio beat him at Zama in 202 BC. Liddell Hart wrote a biography of Scipio in the 1920s and admired him above almost anyone. It became the pattern of his whole life's argument: the quickest way to remove a threat on your doorstep can be to strike at what it depends on somewhere else.
biz: Take the line of least expectation in your marketing

Big lenders and comparison sites spend heavily on the most generic secured loan searches, and fighting them there is the Somme in an ad auction. Go round instead. Build SEO pages that answer specific homeowner questions, such as raising money for home improvements without remortgaging, and test the longer, more specific search phrases where intent is clearer and competition thinner, suggesting these to whoever runs the accounts. Every page must carry the secured lending risk warning and make no promise of approval or rates. Measure cost per completed case by keyword group and by page, not just clicks, and shift effort to the groups that win.
Never renew an attack along the same line

His last maxim says do not repeat an attack in the same form after it has failed. With leads who go quiet, repeated identical calls are both ineffective and, done too often, a form of pressure that Consumer Duty frowns on. Change the form instead of the volume: one short WhatsApp offering a time to talk or an easy way to say no thanks, then a plain email summary, then stop. Set a written maximum number of attempts. Track response rate by contact method and by attempt number, and you will usually find the third identical call adds nothing but annoyance.
connects: Ries and Trout's flanking attack, avoiding the market leader's strength to win an unoccupied position, is Liddell Hart's indirect approach moved from the battlefield to the customer's mind.
Liddell Hart's quiet editing of his record to look more prophetic is exactly the hindsight bias that Tetlock says forecasters must track and correct with honest scorekeeping.
His line of least expectation is a modern restatement of Sun Tzu's advice to avoid strength, strike weakness and appear where you are not expected.
recap:
On the first day of the Battle of the Somme, the first of July nineteen sixteen, the British army suffered about fifty-seven thousand casualties, the worst day in its history. Men walked forward in straight lines into barbed wire and machine guns. A young officer named Basil Liddell Hart, a minister's son who had left Cambridge without a degree, was in those battles, and weeks later he was gassed near Mametz Wood and sent home. He never fought again. But the picture of the straight line into fire stayed with him for life.

He became a military journalist, first for the Daily Telegraph and then for The Times, and one of the most influential voices on defence in Britain. He studied about thirty wars and, by his count, two hundred and eighty campaigns, and he reached a striking conclusion. Decisive results rarely came from a direct attack on the enemy's main army. They came from going round.

That is the first big idea, the indirect approach. A frontal assault hardens resistance, just as pushing on a door makes the person behind it push back.

The second is dislocation. Move against the enemy's rear, his supplies, his line of retreat, so that his position stops making sense and he feels trapped. Beat him in his head first.

The third is the line of least expectation. Where he does not expect you, he is weakest. Threaten more than one target so he cannot tell which you mean. And never renew an attack in the same form after it has failed. That is the Somme in one sentence.

The fourth is grand strategy. The object of war is a better peace, so a total victory that exhausts you and poisons the peace is a kind of defeat.

His friend Lawrence of Arabia seemed to prove it, blowing up a desert railway so the Turks had to defend everything at once.

But the story has a dark turn, and it is the fifth lesson. After the Second World War, a passage praising Liddell Hart appeared in the English edition of a German general's memoir. It was not in the German original. Decades later, a scholar showed from Liddell Hart's own papers that he had encouraged it. He had polished his legend, and it worked for years. The man who taught perception management had been managing ours.

He was knighted in nineteen sixty-six and died in nineteen seventy, a brilliant populariser whose ideas were sometimes better than his honesty.

The line to remember: go round the wall, and check who built the legend.
